headline: The guard told off Hegseth. He got a medal.
summary: On Veterans Day a laugh broke out while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his aides posed for photos at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The sentinel on duty, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, loudly told them off. On Thursday Hegseth pinned the Joint Service Commendation Medal on him, an award that rarely goes to a soldier that junior.
cover_answer: No sorry on record. He posted "Well done, Specialist."
table_question: If someone tells you off and they're right, do you thank them?

5-7.script: A soldier guards a grave for soldiers nobody could name, and the rule there is hush, like a library. On Wednesday the man in charge of all the soldiers took pictures there, someone laughed, and the guard told them off. The next day that boss pinned a medal on him. Doing the job right won.
5-7.why: The hush rule they know best, kept by the guard, and a medal to prove it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a soldier shouting at grown-ups is the loud part they will keep. The script puts the rule first, the library hush they already live under, so the shout is the rule and the medal is the proof. Expect "did he get in trouble?" No. The boss pinned it on himself.

8-12.script: Pete Hegseth runs the Pentagon, so every soldier works for him. On Veterans Day a laugh broke out while he and his aides posed at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and the sentinel told them off. Thursday Hegseth pinned a medal on him. A lifeguard whistles at the pool's owner, and gets a raise.
8-12.why: Rules that reach the top: the chain they check hardest.
8-12.why_long: At ten they are working out whether adults apply the rules to themselves, and mostly catch them not. Here the chain runs clean: the rule, the boss breaking it, a junior soldier enforcing it, the boss handing over a medal for it. The lifeguard and the pool owner is that chain at a size they know. Expect "did he have to?" No.

13-17.script: Was the medal an apology? A laugh broke out while Pete Hegseth and his aides posed at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, the sentinel told them off, and two days later Hegseth gave him a rare medal. Second: the video came a day after he beat an impeachment vote. Does that shrink it?
13-17.why: An apology and a good story for a bad week can both be true.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the guard was right and the medal says so, and a man a day past an impeachment vote needed a good story. The script asks whether the second cancels the first. It does not. Expect "why not just say sorry?" The report has no apology, only "well done", and whether that is enough is theirs to argue.

5-7.a: No. The next day he pinned a medal on the guard and said well done.

8-12.q: Why did the guard yell at the boss?
8-12.a: A laugh broke out during photos. The tomb's quiet rule applies to anyone.

8-12.q: Is the medal a big deal?
8-12.a: Yes. That medal rarely goes to a soldier as junior as a specialist.

13-17.a: No sorry on record. He posted the photos himself: well done, Specialist.

13-17.q: Does it matter that it was impeachment week?
13-17.a: Vote Tuesday, video Wednesday, medal Thursday. Timing isn't motive.
